gallery.title: Size & growth
gallery.blurb: How much research is there? 50,281 records passed the bucket screen and were fully extracted (2010–2026).

figs.title: Cumulative growth
figs.caption: Cumulative records analysed by publication year. Volume grew 28.9× since 2010 — half of all 47,348 full-year records were published 2019 or later.

gallery.title: Financing functions & outcomes
gallery.blurb: The core classification: which health-financing function(s) each study addresses, and which health-system outcome domain(s) it investigates. A study can carry more than one of each, so it is counted in every one it's tagged with.

figs.title: Financing function
figs.caption: Studies by financing function — a study can carry more than one. Benefits decisions leads at 15,791 studies, 1.2× Purchasing's 13,014; capital-investment financing trails furthest behind.

figs.title: Financing-function mix over time
figs.caption: Share of tagged studies by year, top 5 functions; a study can carry more than one, so bars exceed 100%. Benefits decisions's share moved only from 33% to 32% across the whole period — no function's relative weight shifted sharply.

figs.title: Financing-function mix over time (line option)
figs.caption: Share of tagged studies by year, top 5 functions, shown as separate lines; a study can carry more than one, so totals can exceed 100%. Benefits decisions's share moved only from 33% to 32% across the whole period — the alternative view tells the same story as the stacked bars.

figs.title: Financing-function output over time
figs.caption: Annual count of financing-function tags, by function (a study can carry more than one, so totals exceed the study count). Total tags grew 2.2× from 2010 to 2025; Benefits decisions's share moved from 24% to 23% of that total.

figs.title: Outcome domain
figs.caption: Studies by outcome domain — a study can carry more than one. Other is tagged 1.9× as often as Efficiency in the use of resources (22,506 vs 11,776), the next largest domain.

figs.title: Outcome domain (lollipop option)
figs.caption: Alternative view: lollipop chart of studies by outcome domain — a study can carry more than one. Other is tagged 1.9× as often as Efficiency in the use of resources (22,506 vs 11,776), the next largest domain.

figs.title: Function vs. outcome
figs.caption: Outcome-domain mix of each financing function's tagged studies (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag of either kind, so rows needn't sum to 100%). 59% of Capital investment: other health system inputs studies report Other, its most common outcome.

gallery.title: Topics & themes
gallery.blurb: What the research is actually about, beyond the financing-function labels: an OpenAlex-style field/subfield taxonomy, plus an emergent theme model over the abstract text (sentence embeddings → UMAP → HDBSCAN) — the same techniques HEE used for its topic-landscape figures.

figs.title: Topic landscape
figs.caption: OpenAlex-style topic taxonomy — each bar is a subfield (length = studies), coloured by field. 'Economics and Econometrics' leads at 10,773 studies, 2.1× the next-largest ('General Health Professions', 5,084); Social Sciences accounts for 20,442 of 41,952 studies with a topic label.

figs.title: Topic landscape (treemap)
figs.caption: Same OpenAlex-style topic taxonomy as the circular chart, laid out as a treemap — each rectangle is a subfield (area = studies), grouped and coloured by field/domain. 'Economics and Econometrics' is 26% of 41,952 tagged studies on its own, 2.1× the next-largest subfield ('General Health Professions', 5,084) — area makes that skew legible instead of one spoke dwarfing the rest.

figs.title: The opportunity matrix
figs.caption: For each MeSH-derived disease category, its share of tags for a given financing function, divided by that function's overall share across all disease-tagged studies. Blue = disproportionately more attention; red = disproportionately less. Infectious studies are tagged Recurrent financing (supply chain) 2.1× as often as the disease-tagged average, while Musculoskeletal studies are tagged Revenue Raising only 0.32× as often — the widest gaps in either direction.

figs.title: How each disease area is evaluated
figs.caption: Mix of financing-function tags within each MeSH-derived disease category (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag, so rows needn't sum to 100%). Musculoskeletal leans hardest on Benefits decisions (56% of its tagged studies).

figs.title: The disease focus of HFF research
figs.caption: Each bar is a MeSH-derived disease category; length is its share of the disease-coded literature, colour is whether that research skews toward richer or poorer countries. Maternal & neonatal research skews most toward LMICs (63% LMIC); Musculoskeletal skews most toward high-income settings (93% high-income).

figs.title: LMIC research: communicable to NCD shift
figs.caption: Disease mix of MeSH-classified HFF research about low- and middle-income countries, across three epidemiological-transition classes. Communicable/maternal/nutritional fell 82%→49%; non-communicable rose 18%→48%, 2010–2025.

figs.title: Evidence flow: design to function to outcome
figs.caption: Each ribbon is a group of studies flowing from study design, through primary financing function, to primary outcome domain (first-listed tag of each). Ribbon width is the study count. Benefits decisions is the largest single financing-function node (14,176 studies), feeding most often into Other (17,511 studies primarily reporting it).

figs.title: The disease atlas
figs.caption: HFF studies naming each country, split by MeSH-derived disease area (busiest first). Log scale. 'Infectious' research reaches the widest set of countries (115 named); several disease areas stay concentrated in a handful of systems.

figs.title: LMIC research share, era 1 to era 2
figs.caption: Share of research about LMICs within each MeSH-derived disease category, 2010–2017 (dot) to 2018–2026 (arrowhead). Skin's LMIC share rose +21pp; Infectious's fell -14pp — the widest swings either way.

figs.title: Thematic landscape
figs.caption: Abstract embeddings, UMAP + HDBSCAN — each point is one study, positioned by similarity. 'insurance / medicaid / medicare' is the largest emergent theme at 9,317 studies; the top 12 themes shown here cover about 64% of all topic-embedded studies.

figs.title: Top 20 research themes
figs.caption: Top 20 research themes, ranked by cluster size (keyword labels, not hand-assigned categories). 'insurance / medicaid / medicare' leads at 9,317 studies, 1.5× the next-largest ('patients / drug / drugs', 6,030).

figs.title: Themes by income skew
figs.caption: The emergent theme map, each theme coloured by the share of its single-country studies about LMICs (overall 37%). 'insurance / vietnam / coverage' skews most LMIC (100%); 'sud / treatment / substance' skews most high-income (100% high-income).

gallery.title: Methods & data
gallery.blurb: How the research was done: study design, whether the analysis is quantitative, qualitative or mixed, and what kind of data it draws on.

figs.title: Study design
figs.caption: Study design of the analysis population. Cross-sectional and correlational analyses leads at 14,414 studies, well ahead of Experimental and quasi-experimental impact evaluations's 7,908.

figs.title: Type of analysis
figs.caption: Type of analysis, deduced from the abstract text. 79.3% of studies use a quantitative analysis — qualitative and mixed-methods work together make up the remaining 20.7%.

figs.title: Data type
figs.caption: Data type used by the analysis population. Cross-sectional data leads at 18,516 studies, ahead of Time-series / longitudinal's 11,362.

figs.title: Data source
figs.caption: Data source used by the analysis population. Administrative data leads at 18,610 studies, ahead of Primary survey data's 11,163.

gallery.title: Geography
gallery.blurb: Where the research is about. 153 countries are named in the extracted geography.

figs.title: Top 20 countries
figs.caption: Top 20 countries by study count — a multi-country study is counted once per country it names. United States of America leads with 14,487 study-country pairs, 4.1× China's 3,530.

figs.title: Study-country pairs by income group
figs.caption: Study-country pairs by income group. High income accounts for 28,231 study-country pairs, ahead of Upper middle income's 9,426.

figs.title: Geographic scope
figs.caption: Geographic scope of the analysis population. 81.9% of studies name a single country; the rest are multi-country or region/global in scope.

figs.title: Research intensity vs. disease burden
figs.caption: Each point is a country: research intensity (studies per unit of disease burden) against total burden. The median high-income country has 11× more HFF studies per 100,000 DALYs than the median low-income country.

figs.title: Studies vs. a burden-proportional share
figs.caption: If research were proportional to disease burden, each country would hold a share of studies equal to its share of global DALYs. Bars right = below that expected count; left = above. India has about 6,192 fewer studies than a burden-proportional share; the largest surplus sits in United States of America (+12,478).

figs.title: LMIC research share over time
figs.caption: Share of each year's single-country studies that are about low- and middle-income countries. It climbed from 25% in 2010 to 43% in 2025 — real progress, yet still far below the 83% of global disease burden LMICs carry.

figs.title: Evidence concentration among LMICs
figs.caption: Low- and middle-income countries ordered from least to most research per unit of disease burden. The five most-studied LMICs hold 46% of the LMIC evidence (Gini = 0.42).

figs.title: High burden, low research
figs.caption: Each point is a country. The dashed line marks research in proportion to disease burden. 86 of 152 countries sit below the proportionality line; 62% of those are low- or lower-middle-income.

figs.title: Funding priority scorecard
figs.caption: Where economic evidence is most absent relative to disease burden (left), and the 12 countries with the largest absolute shortfall (right). India alone is 6,192 studies short of a burden-proportional share — the largest gap of any country.

figs.title: When evidence reached each income group
figs.caption: Cumulative share of each World Bank income group's countries with ≥1 HFF study naming it, by year. Low income countries reached full coverage first, by 2016; every income group passed 95% coverage by 2020.

figs.title: Biggest producers vs. best-served
figs.caption: The 15 countries with the most HFF studies, ranked by total volume and again per 10 million people. A line falling to the right is a country whose standing rests on its size. India falls from rank 4 to 124 per capita; Netherlands climbs from 14 to 7.

figs.title: Adjusted odds ratios by income group
figs.caption: Adjusted odds ratios from two logistic models on single-country studies with a known income group. Reference group is high-income studies (OR=1). Adjusted for era; observational, so associations not causes. Low income studies have 0.30× the odds of a high-income study of using a quantitative analysis, and 0.08× the odds of Low income studies having a local author.

figs.title: Who leads research about each setting
figs.caption: Author-affiliation pattern of single-country studies, by the income group studied. Only 20% of Low income studies have a local-only author team, and 28% have no local author at all.

figs.title: Local authorship, by financing function
figs.caption: Share of single-country studies with a local author, by financing function tag. Only 89% of Capital investment: infrastructure studies have a local author, vs. 95% for Purchasing.

figs.title: Local authorship, by outcome domain
figs.caption: Authorship pattern of single-country studies reporting each outcome domain (row shares). Only 55% of Transparency and accountability studies have a local-only author team, the lowest share of any outcome domain.

figs.title: Cross-income co-authorship
figs.caption: Cross-income co-authorship of 35,370 studies with a known author-affiliation country. Ribbons: studies co-authored across two income groups (within-group studies excluded from the ribbons). Most evidence isn't cross-income at all: 22,333 studies are wholly high-income-authored; just 260 wholly low-income.

figs.title: Where to build local research capacity
figs.caption: Each country by disease burden and the share of its studies with a local author. Madagascar: high burden, only 47% local authorship.

figs.title: The top research funders
figs.caption: The most-named research funders across studies that report one, after merging name variants into a single entry. National Natural Science Foundation of China is named by 532 studies, more than any other funder.

figs.title: The top research funders (treemap option)
figs.caption: Alternative view: the same top funders shown as a treemap after merging name variants into single entries. National Natural Science Foundation of China is named by 532 studies, more than any other funder.

figs.title: What each top funder pays for
figs.caption: Each top funder's financing-function tag mix (share of that funder's tag mentions; a study can carry more than one tag). 52% of National Institute on Drug Abuse's financing-function tags are Benefits decisions, its most concentrated pairing among the top 12 funders.

figs.title: What each top funder pays for (bubble option)
figs.caption: Alternative view: bubble matrix of each top funder's financing-function mix. Bubble size and colour intensity both reflect the share of that funder's studies; highlighted bubbles show the largest 1–2 shares in each row. 52% of National Institute on Drug Abuse-funded studies are tagged Benefits decisions, its top financing function.

figs.title: What each top funder's research finds
figs.caption: Outcome-domain mix of each top funder's studies (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag, so rows needn't sum to 100%). 66% of National Cancer Institute-funded studies report Other, its most common outcome.

figs.title: Financing-function mix by top funder
figs.caption: Each top funder's financing-function tag mix (share of that funder's tag mentions; a study can carry more than one tag). 35% of Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's financing-function tags are Purchasing, its most concentrated pairing among the top 8 funders.

figs.title: Which funders are gaining ground
figs.caption: Each top funder's share of that year's studies with a known funder, 2013–2025. National Natural Science Foundation of China's share rose +3.7pp from 2013–16 to 2022–25; Canadian Institutes of Health Research's fell -0.8pp.

figs.title: Funder to financing function to authorship
figs.caption: Each ribbon is a group of single-funder, single-country studies flowing from research funder, through primary financing function, to authorship pattern. National Natural Science Foundation of China funds the most studies in this flow (175), and 23 of all 557 studies shown (4%) have no local author at all.

figs.title: Where high burden meets low evidence
figs.caption: Each country by its total disease burden (GBD 2023 DALYs) and its count of HFF studies naming it, in tertiles. Deep red = high burden, little research; blue = well-researched relative to burden; dark purple = high on both; cream = low on both. Angola, Chad, Iraq, Somalia, Algeria fall in the highest-burden, lowest-evidence cell — top third globally for disease burden, bottom third for HFF research volume.

figs.title: Research intensity against disease burden (map)
figs.caption: HFF studies naming each country, per 100,000 DALYs of disease burden. Blue: more research per unit of burden than the typical studied country; red: less. The median studied country has 1.30 studies per 100,000 DALYs — rich, small countries cluster far above that line, populous LMICs far below it.

figs.title: Evidence deserts
figs.caption: Countries by number of HFF studies naming them, against the whole map of GBD 2023 burden. Red = a country that carries disease burden but has no HFF study at all. Equatorial Guinea has GBD burden data but zero HFF studies naming it.

figs.title: Where the evidence is youngest
figs.caption: Share of a country's HFF studies published in 2018–2026, the later half of the window (global average 62%). Green = newer, faster-growing evidence base than average; brown = older. The evidence base is growing fastest in the Gulf and parts of Africa; several Latin American and Eastern European countries still carry a majority pre-2018 evidence base.

figs.title: Where the evidence is about
figs.caption: HFF studies naming each country, per 10 million people (log scale), shown on a diverging red–blue scale. North America, Western Europe, Australia and the Gulf are studied far more intensively per capita than South Asia or sub-Saharan Africa — 42.7 studies per 10M people is the median.

figs.title: The dominant type of analysis
figs.caption: The most common type of analysis among each country's HFF studies (≥5 studies). Colour is the modal category. Quantitative is the modal type in 142 of 144 countries with enough studies to classify — Qualitative leads in only 2.

figs.title: Who studies whom
figs.caption: Share of a country's single-country HFF studies that have at least one author based there. Blue = mostly domestic; red = mostly produced from outside. Haiti has the lowest local-authorship share (17%) among countries with ≥5 studies with a known affiliation.

gallery.title: Global financing context
gallery.blurb: The real-world backdrop for the Revenue Raising financing function: how much development assistance for health (DAH) actually flows, who provides it, and how unequally countries fund their own health spending. Source: IHME, Financing Global Health 2025: Cuts in Aid and Future Outlook.

figs.title: Development assistance for health, 1990–2030
figs.caption: Development assistance for health (DAH), 1990–2030 — solid is historical/preliminary, dashed is forecast. DAH fell 51% from its 2021 peak ($80bn) to $39bn in 2025, and is forecast to stay flat through 2030.

figs.title: The 2025 aid cuts, by source
figs.caption: Change in development assistance for health by source, 2024 → 2025. The US cut $9.5bn (-66%) — alone larger than the $11.0bn net drop across all sources combined.

figs.title: Health spending per person, by income group
figs.caption: Total health spending per person by World Bank income group, 2000–2030 (log scale; dashed = forecast). By 2025, the average person in a high-income country has $7,006 spent on their health — 174× the $40 in a low-income country, where per-person spending has fallen since 2020 ($52).

figs.title: Revenue-Raising research vs. real-world aid
figs.caption: Studies tagged Revenue Raising per year (this dataset) vs. global DAH (IHME), 2010–2025. Revenue-Raising research volume tracks the real DAH trend (correlation r=0.64) — both rose through the 2010s and have pulled back since the DAH peak.

figs.title: Every financing function vs. real-world aid
figs.caption: Growth index (2010–2011=100) for the 6 largest financing functions' study counts, vs. global DAH, 2010–2025. Revenue Raising correlates with the DAH trend at r=0.64, the closest match among the 6 largest financing functions.

figs.title: Aid vs. evidence, by region
figs.caption: Share of global DAH (2022–24 average) vs. share of this dataset's study-country pairs, by region (income-first approximation of GBD super-regions). Sub-Saharan Africa receives 53% of DAH but only 11% of study-country pairs — the largest aid-to-evidence gap of any region.

figs.title: Research intensity vs. health spending, by country
figs.caption: Studies per million people vs. health spending per person (2025), by country. Log-log correlation r=0.61 across 150 matched countries — richer-spending countries are studied far more intensively per capita.

figs.title: Each function's research share vs. health spending
figs.caption: Each function's share of a country's classified research vs. health spending per person (log x-axis), one panel per function, with a linear trend line. Benefits decisions's share rises most with spending (r=0.43); Pooling's share falls most (r=-0.32).

figs.title: Ranked: function share vs. health spending
figs.caption: Correlation between each function's share of a country's research and log(health spending per person), across countries. Benefits decisions correlates at r=0.43; Pooling correlates at r=-0.32, the only clearly negative relationship.

figs.title: Ranked: function share vs. health spending (excluding USA)
figs.caption: Correlation between each function's share of a country's research and log(health spending per person), across countries. Studies mapped to the United States of America are excluded before country shares are recalculated. Benefits decisions correlates at r=0.44; Pooling correlates at r=-0.33, the only clearly negative relationship.

figs.title: Paired lollipop: all studies vs excluding USA
figs.caption: Paired lollipops compare each financing function's correlation between country-level research share and log(health spending per person): all studies versus the no-USA sensitivity analysis. The largest shift is for Purchasing (0.15 to 0.12).

figs.title: Correlation sensitivity: all studies vs excluding USA
figs.caption: Each point compares the correlation between a financing function's country-level research share and log(health spending per person) before and after removing all studies mapped to the United States of America. The largest shift is for Purchasing (0.15 to 0.12).

figs.title: Global financing-function mix: all studies vs excluding USA
figs.caption: Each point compares a financing function's share of all classified function tags in the full dataset versus after removing every study mapped to the United States of America. The largest shift is for Purchasing (-3.5 percentage points).

figs.title: Change in financing-function mix after excluding USA
figs.caption: Percentage-point change in each function's share of all classified function tags after removing every study mapped to the United States of America. Purchasing changes the most (-3.5 percentage points), showing how small the overall composition shift is.

figs.title: Financing-function mix by spending quartile
figs.caption: Financing-function mix (% of classified research) by health-spending quartile. Benefits decisions's share rises +10.6pp from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile, while Revenue Raising's share falls -7.3pp.

figs.title: Outcome-domain mix by spending quartile
figs.caption: Outcome-domain mix (% of classified research) by health-spending quartile. Efficiency in resource use's share rises +6.7pp from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile, while Financial protection's share falls -7.8pp.

figs.title: Financing-function ranks, aid boom vs. bust
figs.caption: Rank of each function's average annual study count, DAH boom era (2015–2019) vs. bust era (2022–2025). Public financial management climbed from rank 3 to 2; Purchasing fell from rank 2 to 3.

gallery.title: Pipeline
gallery.blurb: How the dataset itself was built — from the bucket screen through extraction to DOI and topic-theme recovery. See the Methods tab for the full stage-by-stage funnel and what each stage means.

figs.title: Pipeline funnel
figs.caption: Pipeline stage counts, from bucket screen to topic-theme recovery. 95.2% of 52,826 bucket-screened records were fully extracted (50,281); 83.4% of those also got a MeSH or topic theme.
